title: Episode 5 (lines 924–1053)

teacherSummary.text: The blind prophet Teiresias warns Creon that the birds and altars show the gods' anger: the unburied body pollutes the city. He urges Creon to yield. Creon insults him as a money-getter. Teiresias prophesies that Creon will pay with a child of his own. Shaken, Creon decides to bury Polyneices and free Antigone.

context.history: Teiresias, the same seer as in Oedipus Rex, brings the gods' judgment. Signs from birds and sacrifices were standard means of divination.

significance: Creon finally bends, but too late. The play's lesson, "To err is common," is offered and almost accepted.

Old man, ye all let fly at me your shafts
Like anchors at a target; yea, ye set
Your soothsayer on me. Peddlers are ye all
And I the merchandise ye buy and sell.
Go to, and make your profit where ye will,
Silver of Sardis change for gold of Ind;
Ye will not purchase this man’s burial,
Not though the wingèd ministers of Zeus
Should bear him in their talons to his throne;
Not e’en in awe of prodigy so dire
Would I permit his burial, for I know
No human soilure can assail the gods;
This too I know, Teiresias, dire’s the fall
Of craft and cunning when it tries to gloss
Foul treachery with fair words for filthy gain.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “O ponder this, my son. To err is common / To all men, but the man who having erred / Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks / The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.” slowly and put it in my own words: Teiresias tells Creon that everyone makes mistakes; the man who does not cling to his error but repents and seeks a cure is neither foolish nor worthless. Next, craft. I notice he speaks gently, my son, and frames his warning as a truth about all men. The strongest word is “errors”: the word turns Creon's crime into something every person shares. Then, effect. Why does Teiresias frame his warning to Creon as a general truth about error? My answer: Teiresias frames his warning as a general truth about error so that Creon can yield without shame: if every man errs, then repenting is wisdom, not weakness; Creon answers by insulting the prophet.
